conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s a quick, 10-question check-in that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally since your baby arrived. Anything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team—no judgment, just support. We’ll go at your pace, and if any question feels hard, we can pause or talk it through. Ready to begin?

In the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly? Not much. I used to laugh all the time—my husband and I would joke around every night—but lately, even when he tries, it feels like I’m faking it. Maybe once or twice this week I let out a real laugh, but it fizzles fast and then I feel guilty for even enjoying anything when I’m supposed to be focused on the baby.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes… but it’s like the laughter gets stuck. My sister sent a silly video yesterday and I felt a tiny spark, but it faded right away and I went back to feeling flat. So, I guess “not very often” is the truth.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even a shower without interruption—but now it all feels like one more chore. I keep telling myself I should want to do them, but the spark just isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… pretty often. If the baby won’t settle, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—maybe I’m not holding him right or I missed some cue. When I spilled a bottle of pumped milk last night, I sat on the kitchen floor crying, telling myself I’m a terrible mom for wasting it. I know it’s just milk, but in my head it feels like proof I’m failing.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

All the time. Even when the baby’s sleeping peacefully, I’m checking every few minutes to make sure he’s still breathing. Last night I got up three times just to feel his chest rise. I know it sounds crazy, but if I hear the tiniest grunt on the monitor my heart starts racing and I can’t settle down again.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week it’s hit me out of nowhere—like yesterday afternoon, I was folding laundry and suddenly my chest got tight, heart pounding, this wave of “something awful is about to happen.” I knew it wasn’t logical, but I still had to put the basket down and sit because I felt dizzy. It passed after a couple of minutes, but it left me shaky the rest of the day.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days. Between feedings, diapers, trying to shower, the house being a mess, and feeling like I should be grateful—it all piles up until I’m sitting on the couch with the baby in my arms just staring at the wall, not sure what to tackle next. I usually push through, but it feels like I’m wading through thick mud just to get the basics done.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… the unhappiness keeps me up. I’ll lie there after a night-feed, baby already back asleep, but my mind just spins—worrying I did something wrong, replaying every little grunt or cry, feeling guilty for wanting just a few hours of rest. Some nights I watch the clock slide past two, then three, and still can’t drift off.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. I wake up with this heavy feeling in my chest, like there’s a weight I can’t shake off. Even when the baby smiles or something nice happens, the sadness is still sitting right underneath, and by evening it’s back to the front. I keep telling myself I should be happy—he’s healthy, I’m okay—but the miserable feeling just lingers.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

A few times—usually after the baby finally goes down and the house is quiet. Yesterday I was washing bottles, and out of nowhere tears started pouring. Nothing specific happened; it was just this wave of “I can’t do this.” I ended up sobbing over the sink, trying not to wake anyone. It’s like the sadness needs an exit and the only way it knows is crying.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… never. I might feel overwhelmed and cry, but hurting myself has never crossed my mind. I just want to feel better for my baby’s sake—and for mine.

You've shared that over the past week laughter and excitement feel almost out of reach, replaced by a heavy, lingering sadness and constant worry about your baby's wellbeing. <quote>I wake up with this weight I can't shake</quote> and <quote>I ended up sobbing over the sink</quote> paint a picture of deep emotional exhaustion, yet you're still showing up for your little one, trying to push through the mud even when everything feels like one more chore.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 22, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only rare, fleeting moments of amusement that fade quickly, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, describing even previously enjoyable activities as burdensome chores with no spark</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent self-blame for routine infant-care issues and equates minor mishaps with maternal failure, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, intrusive worry with compulsive checking and physiological arousal, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden panic with physical symptoms (tight chest, pounding heart, dizziness) occurring "a few times this week," matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling overwhelmed on "most days" and struggling to manage basic tasks, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent sleep difficulty 'most of the time' due to unhappiness, lying awake for hours with racing thoughts and guilt.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive daily sadness that persists despite positive moments, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 22 places you well above the 14 threshold indicating probable <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> and co-occurring <med>anxiety</med>. You endorse daily <sym>anhedonia</sym> (Q1-2, score 5/6), near-constant <sym>self-blame</sym> (Q3, score 3), pervasive <sym>worry and nocturnal hyper-arousal</sym> (Q4-7, scores 8/9), and frequent <sym>panic-type episodes</sym>. These patterns, combined with <sym>middle-of-the-night crying spells</sym> and the subjective sense of drowning in routine tasks, align with DSM-5 criteria for moderate-severe depression and an anxiety specifier. <quote>I should be grateful… but the miserable feeling just lingers</quote> captures the marked distress and functional impairment typical at this severity. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> to review results and discuss treatment options
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for comprehensive evaluation and therapy
3. Consider evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or, if indicated, <med>sertraline</med> or other breastfeeding-compatible antidepressants
4. Practice 15-20 min daily of paced breathing or guided mindfulness to reduce <sym>panic symptoms</sym>
5. Share nighttime infant duties with partner or support person to secure 4-5 hr blocks of sleep
6. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor progress
7. Keep local <med>postpartum support group</med> numbers handy for daytime encouragement
8. If thoughts of self-harm ever emerge, call 988 (U.S.) or your local emergency services immediately
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 22: Post-partum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
(Responses to 10-item EPDS-equivalent questionnaire)

Date: [today]

Symptoms endorsed (present >50% of days):  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness (Q8, Q9)  
- Anhedonia & loss of anticipatory pleasure (Q1, Q2)  
- Excessive guilt/self-blame (Q3)  
- Free-floating anxiety, nocturnal hyper-arousal, panic-type episodes (Q4, Q5, Q7)  
- Subjective overwhelm & impaired coping (Q6)  
- Sleep disruption secondary to rumination (Q7)

Patterns:  
Consistent dysphoric-anxious presentation; no diurnal variation noted; functioning impaired but infant care maintained.

Risk indicators:  
- High postpartum anxiety (panic attacks, compulsive checking)  
- Moderate–severe depressive symptoms (sadness, guilt, anhedonia)  
- Sleep deprivation compounding mood liability  
- No self-harm ideation (Q10 negative) → no acute safety concern on basis of these responses

Screening significance:  
Score profile suggests clinically significant postpartum depression with prominent anxiety features; warrants formal assessment (EPDS/PHQ-9/GAD-7) and possible referral to perinatal mental health specialty for evaluation and treatment planning.

No immediate safety alert at this time.
